at falde.explanation: "At falde" means "to fall", for example to fall down, or for rain and snow to fall. "Jeg faldt på cyklen" means "I fell off my bike" (literally "on the bike"). Danes also say "falde i søvn" (to fall asleep).

sentence.en: Careful, you're going to fall!

at finde.explanation: "At finde" means "to find", whether you look for something or come across it: "Jeg finder mine nøgler" (I find my keys). It is also used for opinions: "Jeg finder det svært" (I find it difficult). The opposite is "at miste" (to lose something), while "at tabe" (to lose) is for losing a game.

sentence.en: I can't find my keys.

at flytte.explanation: "At flytte" means "to move", either to a new home or to shift something from one place to another. "Vi flytter til Aarhus" means "We are moving to Aarhus", and "Kan du flytte bilen?" means "Can you move the car?".

sentence.da: Vi **flytter** til en ny lejlighed i næste måned.
sentence.en: We are moving to a new flat next month.

at flyve.explanation: "At flyve" means "to fly", for birds and for people travelling by plane: "Vi flyver til Spanien" (We are flying to Spain). The plane itself is "et fly" (a plane).

sentence.en: We are flying to Spain this summer.

at forhandle.explanation: "At forhandle" means "to negotiate", for example prices, contracts or pay. You negotiate about something with "om" (about): "forhandle om prisen" (negotiate the price). Be careful: "en forhandler" is not a negotiator but a dealer or retailer, such as a car dealer.

sentence.en: They are going to negotiate the price.

at forklare.explanation: "At forklare" means "to explain". Danish says "forklare noget for nogen" (explain something to someone): "Kan du forklare det for mig?" (Can you explain it to me?). A handy phrase for learners is "Kan du forklare det igen?" (Can you explain it again?).

sentence.en: Can you explain it again, please?

at forstå.explanation: "At forstå" means "to understand": "Jeg forstår ikke" (I don't understand). A handy follow-up when someone speaks too fast is "Kan du gentage det?" (Can you repeat that?).

sentence.en: I don't understand the question.

at fortælle.explanation: "At fortælle" means "to tell", especially to tell a story or give someone information. "At sige" (to say) is for simply saying something, while "fortælle" is for telling more. You can add who you tell: "fortælle nogen noget" (tell someone something).

sentence.en: My grandmother tells a story.

at fryse.explanation: "At fryse" means "to freeze" and also "to feel cold". "Jeg fryser" means "I am cold" (literally "I freeze"). It also describes water or food turning to ice. The appliance that keeps food frozen is "en fryser" (a freezer).

sentence.en: I am cold because it is chilly.

at fylde år.explanation: "At fylde år" means "to have a birthday", in the sense of turning a certain age. You can add the age: "Jeg fylder tredive år" (I am turning thirty). "At have fødselsdag" (to have a birthday) just says it is your birthday, without the age.

sentence.en: My dad has a birthday tomorrow.

at få.explanation: "At få" means "to get" or "to receive": "Jeg får en gave" (I get a present). It is also used for "to be allowed to": "Jeg fik lov" (I was allowed). It does not mean to go and fetch something. That is "at hente" (to fetch).

sentence.da: Jeg **får** en gave til min fødselsdag.
sentence.en: I get a present for my birthday.

at få hjælp.explanation: "At få hjælp" means "to get help", that is, to receive it from someone. To give help, say "at hjælpe" (to help). A very useful phrase is "Jeg har brug for hjælp" (I need help). Danish says "hjælp" with no "a" in front.

sentence.en: I can get help at the office.

at føle.explanation: "At føle" means "to feel", both emotions and things you touch. To say how you feel, add "mig" (myself): "Jeg føler mig glad" means "I feel happy".

sentence.en: I feel happy today.

en familie.explanation: "En familie" means "a family". Say "min familie" for "my family". A friendly question is "Har du en stor familie?" (Do you have a big family?).

sentence.en: My family lives in Aarhus.

en far.explanation: "En far" means "a father". "Far" is also used like a name when you speak to him: "Hej, far!" (Hi, Dad!). The matching word for a mother is "en mor" (a mother).

sentence.en: My father works at a hospital.

en farfar.explanation: "En farfar" means "a grandfather" on your father's side, literally "father-father". Danish keeps the four grandparents apart: "mormor" (mother's mother), "morfar" (mother's father), "farmor" (father's mother) and "farfar" (father's father). Children use "Farfar" like a name.

sentence.en: My grandfather is eighty years old.

en farmor.explanation: "En farmor" means "a grandmother" on your father's side. It is made from "far" (father) and "mor" (mother). The word for your mother's mother is "mormor" (mother's mother). Danes use these words like names, so you will hear "Farmor kommer i dag" (Grandma is coming today).

sentence.en: My grandmother bakes good buns.

en farve.explanation: "En farve" means "a color". In a shop you may ask "Har I den i en anden farve?" (Do you have it in another color?). "Hvilken farve" means "what color". "Farve" is also used for hair dye or paint.

sentence.en: Which color do you like best?

en feber.explanation: "En feber" means "a fever", a high body temperature when you are sick. Danes say "Jeg har feber" (I have a fever), usually without "en".

sentence.da: Hun har **feber** og bliver i sengen.
sentence.en: She has a fever and stays in bed.

en ferie.explanation: "En ferie" means "a vacation" or holiday, a time away from work or school. You say "på ferie" (on vacation): "Jeg er på ferie" (I am on vacation). "I ferien" means "during the vacation", and "sommerferie" means "summer vacation".

sentence.en: We are going on vacation in July.

en fest.explanation: "En fest" means "a party" or a celebration. You say "at holde fest" (to have a party) or "at gå til fest" (to go to a party). "God fest!" means "Have a good party!".

sentence.en: We are having a party on Saturday.

en film.explanation: "En film" means "a film" or "a movie". The plural is just "film", so "to film" means "two films" ("to" is the number two). Typical phrases are "at se en film" (to watch a film) and "en dansk film" (a Danish film).

sentence.da: Vi ser en god **film** i aften.
sentence.en: We are watching a good film tonight.

en finger.explanation: "En finger" means "a finger". The thumb is "tommelfingeren" (the thumb) and the index finger is "pegefingeren" (the index finger). Danish says "the finger" where English says "my finger": "Jeg har ondt i fingeren" means "I have a pain in the finger", i.e. "my finger hurts".

sentence.en: I have cut my finger.

en fisk.explanation: "En fisk" means "a fish", both the animal in the water and the food on your plate. As in English, the plural can be the same word as the single one: "tre fisk" (three fish). "At fiske" means "to fish".

sentence.en: I eat fish every Friday.

en flaske.explanation: "En flaske" means "a bottle". Danish has no word for "of" here: "en flaske vand" is "a bottle of water", and "et glas vand" is "a glass of water".

sentence.en: I am buying a bottle of water.

en flybillet.explanation: "En flybillet" means "a plane ticket". It is built from "fly" (plane) and "billet" (ticket). You buy one with "at købe en flybillet" (to buy a plane ticket).

sentence.da: Jeg har købt **en flybillet** til Paris.
sentence.en: I have bought a plane ticket to Paris.

en fod.explanation: "En fod" means "a foot". "Til fods" means "on foot" (walking). Danish says "the feet" where English says "my feet": "Jeg har ondt i fødderne" is "I have a pain in the feet", meaning "my feet hurt".

sentence.en: My feet are cold.

en forfader.explanation: "En forfader" means "an ancestor". It is a little formal. For the nearest generations Danes often say "mine oldeforældre" (my great-grandparents).

sentence.en: My ancestor was a farmer in Jutland.

en forkølelse.explanation: "En forkølelse" means "a cold", the illness with a runny nose and a sore throat. In everyday talk Danes more often say "Jeg er forkølet" (I have a cold). Do not mix it up with "kold" (cold in temperature).

sentence.da: Jeg har en **forkølelse** og en hoste.
sentence.en: I have a cold and a cough.

en fornyelse.explanation: "En fornyelse" means "a renewal". You use it for things like passports, contracts and subscriptions. It comes from "at forny" (to renew).

sentence.da: Det er tid til **fornyelse** af kontrakten.
sentence.en: It is time for renewal of the contract.

en forret.explanation: "En forret" means "a starter", the small dish you eat before the main one. The main dish is called "hovedretten" (the main course).

sentence.en: I will have a soup as a starter.

en forsinkelse.explanation: "En forsinkelse" means "a delay", for example a train or flight running late. You hear "Der er forsinkelse" (There is a delay) in announcements. "Toget er forsinket" means "The train is late".

sentence.da: Der er **en forsinkelse** på tyve minutter.
sentence.en: There is a delay of twenty minutes.

en frakke.explanation: "En frakke" means "a coat". It is longer and warmer than "en jakke" (a jacket). To put it on, you say "at tage frakken på" (to put the coat on).

sentence.en: I put my coat on.

en frikadelle.explanation: "En frikadelle" means "a meatball". It is usually flat rather than round, made of pork and fried in a pan.

sentence.en: We eat meatballs with potatoes.

en frisør.explanation: "En frisør" means "a hairdresser", and it also means the place where you get a haircut. "Jeg skal til frisør" means "I am going to the hairdresser". A barber, who cuts men's hair, is "en barber".

sentence.en: I am going to the hairdresser tomorrow.

en frugt.explanation: "En frugt" means "a fruit". For fruit in general Danes usually leave out "en": "Jeg spiser meget frugt" (I eat a lot of fruit). One piece of fruit is "et stykke frugt".

sentence.en: The children eat fruit every day.

en fugl.explanation: "En fugl" means "a bird". It appears in the saying "en fugl i hånden er bedre end ti på taget" (a bird in the hand is better than ten on the roof), the Danish version of "a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush".

sentence.en: There is a bird sitting in the tree.

en fætter.explanation: "En fætter" means "a male cousin", the son of your aunt or uncle. Danish has a separate word for a female cousin, "en kusine", while English uses "cousin" for both.

sentence.en: My cousin is my age.

en fødselsdag.explanation: "En fødselsdag" means "a birthday". The usual greeting is "Tillykke med fødselsdagen!" (Happy birthday!). To ask "When is your birthday?" Danes say "Hvornår har du fødselsdag?", which is literally "When have you birthday?".

sentence.en: When is your birthday?

en fødselsdagsfest.explanation: "En fødselsdagsfest" means "a birthday party". It is built from "fødselsdag" (birthday) and "fest" (party). You say "til en fødselsdagsfest" for "at a birthday party".

sentence.da: Der er **fødselsdagsfest** hos Anna i lørdag.
sentence.en: There is a birthday party at Anna's on Saturday.

en fødselsdagsgave.explanation: "En fødselsdagsgave" means "a birthday present". It is built from "fødselsdag" (birthday) and "gave" (gift). You can also say just "en gave" (a gift), which works for any occasion.

sentence.da: Jeg har købt en **fødselsdagsgave** til min mor.
sentence.en: I have bought a birthday present for my mother.

en fødselsdato.explanation: "En fødselsdato" means "a date of birth", the day, month and year you were born. You see it on forms. It is not the same as "en fødselsdag" (a birthday), the day you celebrate each year.

sentence.en: Write your date of birth here.

et fly.explanation: "Et fly" means "a plane". It is closely related to "at flyve" (to fly). "En flyvemaskine" (an airplane) also exists, but it is longer and "et fly" is the everyday word.

sentence.en: The plane lands at eight o'clock.

et fornavn.explanation: "Et fornavn" means "a first name". It is made of "for" (before) and "et navn" (a name). Many Danes also have "et mellemnavn" (a middle name).

sentence.en: My first name is Anna.

et forår.explanation: "Et forår" means "a spring", the season between winter and summer. You say "om foråret" to mean "in the spring" in general.

sentence.en: The flowers come out in the spring.

et får.explanation: "Et får" means "a sheep". A young sheep is "et lam" (a lamb), and "lammekød" is lamb meat.

sentence.en: The sheep are standing in the field.

et fødested.explanation: "Et fødested" means "a birthplace", the town or country where someone was born. It is made of "fødsel" (birth) and "et sted" (a place). On forms it often sits next to "Fødselsdato" (date of birth).

sentence.en: My birthplace is Odense.

faktisk.explanation: "Faktisk" means "actually" or "in fact". It adds a fact, a surprise or a small correction: "Jeg bor faktisk her" means "I actually live here".

sentence.en: I am actually quite hungry.

fantastisk.explanation: "Fantastisk" means "fantastic" and is used much like in English. It is stronger than "god" (good), so save it for something really great.

sentence.en: It was a fantastic film.

farlig.explanation: "Farlig" means "dangerous" and comes from "fare" (danger). The opposite is "sikker" (safe). On signs you may see "Livsfarlig!", which means "Danger to life!".

sentence.en: The road is very dangerous.

farvel.explanation: "Farvel" means "goodbye". It sounds more final than "hej hej" (bye bye) or "vi ses" (see you), which Danes use for everyday goodbyes. Use "farvel" when you will not see the person for a while.

sentence.en: I say goodbye to my friend.

fattig.explanation: "Fattig" means "poor", with little money, for people and also for countries. The opposite is "rig" (rich). "Stakkels" also means "poor", but in the sense of "unlucky": "stakkels dig" means "poor you".

sentence.da: Han var **fattig**, da han var ung.
sentence.en: He was poor when he was young.

februar.explanation: "Februar" means "February". Month names are written with a small letter in Danish, and the spelling ends in -ar, not -ary: write "februar", not "february".

sentence.en: My birthday is in February.

fem.explanation: "Fem" means "five". "Femten" (fifteen) is built from it, but fifty is not: it is "halvtreds", not "femti".

sentence.en: It's five o'clock.

femogtredive.explanation: "Femogtredive" means "thirty-five". In Danish numbers like 35 the ones come first: "fem-og-tredive" is literally "five-and-thirty". It is written as one word.

sentence.en: My brother is thirty-five years old.

femte.explanation: "Femte" means "fifth". It comes from "fem" (five) and is used for order and dates: "den femte marts" means "the fifth of March".

sentence.en: My birthday is the fifth of March.

femten.explanation: "Femten" means "fifteen". For time, Danes often say "en kvart" (a quarter of an hour) instead of "femten minutter" (fifteen minutes), though both are fine.

sentence.en: There are fifteen students in the class.

fin.explanation: "Fin" means "fine" or "nice", and Danes use it a lot to say something is good. It can also mean "fancy" or "elegant". "Fint!" on its own means "Great!" or "Okay, good!".

sentence.en: It is a nice house.

finland.explanation: "Finland" means "Finland". It is written with a capital letter, as in English. A person from there is "en finne" (a Finn) and the language is "finsk" (Finnish).

sentence.da: Vi skal rejse til **Finland** i vinter.
sentence.en: We are going to travel to Finland this winter.

finsk.explanation: "Finsk" means "Finnish" and describes things from Finland, including the language. Unlike in English, it is written with a small letter. Words ending in -sk take no extra "t" with et-words: "et finsk hus", not "finskt".

sentence.en: My friend eats Finnish food.

fint.explanation: "Fint" means "fine" or "nicely". It is a common answer to "Hvordan går det?" (How is it going?): "Det går fint" means "It is going fine". Saying "Fint!" on its own is a friendly way to agree.

sentence.en: It is going fine, thanks.

fire.explanation: "Fire" means "four". Do not mix it up with "fyrre" (forty), which looks similar. "Fjerde" (fourth) and "fjorten" (fourteen) come from it, but are spelled with "fj" instead of "fi".

sentence.en: I have four brothers.

fireogtyve.explanation: "Fireogtyve" means "twenty-four". It is literally "four-and-twenty": the ones come first. Numbers 21 to 29 work the same way: "treogtyve" (23) and "femogtyve" (25).

sentence.da: Der er **fireogtyve** timer i et døgn.
sentence.en: There are twenty-four hours in a day.

firs.explanation: "Firs" means "eighty". It is short for "firsindstyve", literally "four times twenty", so Danish counts eighty as four twenties. Today people only say "firs".

sentence.en: The house costs eighty thousand kroner.

fjerde.explanation: "Fjerde" means "fourth". It comes from "fire" (four) and is used for order, such as floors, dates and places in a line: "den fjerde maj" means "the fourth of May".

sentence.en: He sat in the fourth row.

fjorten.explanation: "Fjorten" means "fourteen". It comes from "fire" (four), but the spelling changes. "Fjorten dage" (literally "fourteen days") is the usual way to say "two weeks".

sentence.da: Vi tager på ferie i **fjorten** dage.
sentence.en: We're going on holiday for two weeks.

flere.explanation: "Flere" means "more" or "several", for things you can count: "flere biler" means "more cars". For things you cannot count, like water, use "mere" (more). "De fleste" means "most of them".

sentence.en: I have several friends in Denmark.

flot.explanation: "Flot" means "good-looking" or "impressive", for people, clothes, places and even results. Saying "Flot!" to someone means "Well done!".

sentence.en: It is a very nice-looking car.

fløde.explanation: "Fløde" means "cream", the thick, fatty part of milk. It is used in coffee and in cooking: "kaffe med fløde" means "coffee with cream". "Piskefløde" is "whipping cream".

sentence.en: Do you want cream in your coffee?

fodbold.explanation: "Fodbold" means "soccer" (called "football" in British English). The game has no "en" in front: "Jeg spiller fodbold" means "I play soccer". The ball itself is "en fodbold".

sentence.en: My son loves soccer.

for.explanation: "For" has many uses. Before a describing word it means "too": "for varm" (too hot), "for sent" (too late). With "siden" it means "ago": "for to dage siden" is "two days ago". Danish often uses "til" where English says "for": "en gave til dig" means "a gift for you".

sentence.en: The soup is too hot.

forms.da: Jeg kan godt lide frugt, for eksempel æbler.
forms.en: I like fruit, for example apples.

forms.da: Vi kan mødes, for eksempel i morgen.
forms.en: We can meet, for example tomorrow.

for eksempel.explanation: "For eksempel" means "for example" and introduces an example. In writing it is often shortened to "fx" or "f.eks.". It can come in the middle or at the start of a sentence, usually with a small pause.

sentence.da: Jeg kan lide mange sporter, **for eksempel** fodbold.
sentence.en: I like many sports, for example football.

forms.da: For pokker, jeg har glemt nøglen!
forms.en: Darn it, I forgot the key!

for pokker.explanation: "For pokker" is a mild exclamation like "darn it" or "for heaven's sake", used when something annoying or surprising happens. It is harmless, though it sounds a little old-fashioned to younger people. "For søren" is a similar mild one.

sentence.da: **For pokker**, nu har jeg glemt min nøgle!
sentence.en: Darn it, now I've forgotten my key!

foran.explanation: "Foran" means "in front of": "Bilen holder foran huset" means "The car is parked in front of the house". It can also stand alone: "Gå foran" means "Go first". The opposite is "bag" (behind).

sentence.en: The car is parked in front of the house.

forbi.explanation: "Forbi" means "past" or "by": "Han gik forbi huset" means "He walked past the house". It also means "over" or "finished": "Det er forbi" means "It is over". "Komme forbi" means "to drop by": "Kom forbi i aften!" means "Drop by tonight!".

sentence.en: The bus goes past the school.

fordi.explanation: "Fordi" means "because" and gives a reason. It is the usual answer to "hvorfor?" (why?). After "fordi", "ikke" (not) comes before "kan" (can): "fordi jeg ikke kan" means "because I cannot", while a plain sentence says "jeg kan ikke". Do not mix it up with "derfor" (that is why).

sentence.da: Jeg bliver hjemme, **fordi** jeg er syg.
sentence.en: I am staying home because I am sick.

forkert.explanation: "Forkert" means "wrong" or "incorrect", for answers, directions, numbers or choices. It is the opposite of "rigtig" (correct). To say you made a mistake, say "Jeg tog fejl" (I was mistaken).

sentence.en: That is a wrong number.

forkølet.explanation: "Forkølet" means "having a cold". "Jeg er forkølet" means "I have a cold", literally "I am colded". It is milder than "syg" (sick). The illness itself is "en forkølelse".

sentence.en: I have a cold and am staying home.

forsinket.explanation: "Forsinket" means "delayed" or "late", mostly for trains, buses and planes. About yourself you can also say "Jeg er forsinket" (I am late).

sentence.en: The train is delayed by twenty minutes.

forms.en: I am telling you this in confidence

fortroligt.explanation: "Fortroligt" means "confidentially", and also "confidential" before et-words, as in "et fortroligt dokument" (a confidential document). It is common at work, for documents that must not be shared.

sentence.da: Jeg siger det **fortroligt**, så sig det ikke til andre.
sentence.en: I'm telling you in confidence, so don't tell anyone else.

forældre.explanation: "Forældre" means "parents", mother and father together. It is only used for more than one person, so there is no "en" or "et" in front. For one parent, say "en forælder".

sentence.en: My parents live in Aarhus.

fra.explanation: "Fra" means "from", for places, people and the start of a time: "Hvor kommer du fra?" means "Where are you from?". The opposite is "til" (to), and they often go together: "fra mandag til fredag" means "from Monday to Friday".

sentence.en: She comes from Norway.

frankrig.explanation: "Frankrig" means "France". It is written with a capital letter and has no word like "the" in front. A person is "en franskmand" (a Frenchman) and the language is "fransk" (French). The spelling ends in -rig, not -ce.

sentence.en: She is travelling to France this summer.

fransk.explanation: "Fransk" means "French", for things from France and for the language. Unlike in English, it has no capital letter. On menus you may see "fransk løgsuppe" (French onion soup).

sentence.en: I like French cheese.

franskbrød.explanation: "Franskbrød" means "white bread", usually a light loaf made from wheat flour. Danes often compare it with "rugbrød" (rye bread), the dark and heavy kind.

sentence.en: I buy a white loaf at the baker's.

fredag.explanation: "Fredag" means "Friday". "På fredag" means "on Friday" (the coming one) and "om fredagen" means "on Fridays" (every Friday). Day names are written with a small letter.

sentence.en: I am looking forward to Friday.

fri.explanation: "Fri" means "free", as in not tied up, and also "off" from work or school: "Jeg har fri" means "I am off work". It does not mean free of charge; for that use "gratis".

sentence.en: I am off on Friday.

frisk.explanation: "Frisk" means "fresh", and it is used for food and air. It also describes a person who is healthy: "Jeg er frisk" means "I am well". The opposite for food is "gammel" (old, stale).

sentence.en: The bread is fresh.

fritid.explanation: "Fritid" means "free time", the time when you are not at work or school. A very common phrase is "i min fritid" (in my free time), often used when talking about hobbies.

sentence.en: In my free time I read books.

frokost.explanation: "Frokost" means "lunch", the meal around midday. You say "spise frokost" (to eat lunch) and "til frokost" (for lunch). It also names the lunch break at work.

sentence.en: Shall we have lunch together?

frossen.explanation: "Frossen" means "frozen", as in "frossen pizza" (frozen pizza). Do not use it for a person who is cold: for that Danes say "jeg fryser" (I am cold, literally "I freeze").

sentence.en: We have frozen vegetables in the freezer.

fuld.explanation: "Fuld" means "full", for a glass, a bus or a room. When it describes a person, it means "drunk": "Han er fuld" means "He is drunk". To say you are full after a meal, use "mæt" (full after eating). The opposite of "fuld" is "tom" (empty).

sentence.en: The bus is completely full.

fyrre.explanation: "Fyrre" means "forty". Do not mix it up with "fire" (four), which looks similar but is a very different number. In numbers like 41 the ones come first: "enogfyrre" is literally "one-and-forty".

sentence.en: There are forty students at the school.

færdig.explanation: "Færdig" means "finished" or "done". "Jeg er færdig" means "I am done", for example after a meal or at the end of work. It is not the same as "klar" (ready), which means prepared to start. The opposite is "ufærdig" (unfinished).

sentence.da: Jeg er næsten **færdig** med at spise.
sentence.en: I have almost finished eating.

forms.en: Are you finished with the book?

forms.da: Vi er færdige med at spise.

færdig med.explanation: "Færdig med" means "finished with". After "med" (with) you put the thing ("færdig med lektierne", finished with the homework) or an action starting with "at" ("færdig med at spise", finished eating).

sentence.en: I am finished with my homework.

før.explanation: "Før" means "before", and it works for times ("før klokken fem", before five o'clock) and for linking two actions ("før du går", before you go). "Inden" (before) is another everyday word with almost the same meaning. The opposite is "efter" (after).

sentence.en: Call me before five o'clock.

først.explanation: "Først" means "first" in order: "Først spiser vi" (First we eat). It can also mean "not until": "Jeg kommer først i morgen" means "I am not coming until tomorrow". The opposite of the first meaning is "sidst" (last).

sentence.en: First we are going to eat.

første.explanation: "Første" means "first", and it is used in dates: "den første maj" is the first of May. In writing, Danes put a dot after the number, so "1. maj" is read "første maj". Do not mix it up with "først" (first, at first), which is for the order of actions.

sentence.da: Det er min **første** dag på arbejde.
sentence.en: It is my first day at work.
